documents.abstract: Keynote: II International Meeting of UNESCO Chairs in Open, Digital and Distance Education, "Transforming Higher Education: People-Centred Digital Technologies and Artificial Intelligence." Madrid, 18-19 November, 2026.Every educational technology proposes a pedagogy. Jupyter notebooks, for example, by weaving narrative with code, invited a way of teaching computing as storytelling and live exploration; because they are open source, they also encouraged the sharing of learning resources and became ubiquitous. Generative AI proposes a pedagogy too, and its default is troubling: shaped like conversation, in everyday use it reverts to an antiquated model of instruction, the delivery of answers. Students who use AI as an answer machine develop an illusion of competence: the feeling of understanding without its substance. In this talk, I return to first principles. With Piaget and Papert, learners construct knowledge; with Gordon Pask, understanding is demonstrated by explaining it back in conversation; with Andrea diSessa, literacy is a social infrastructure, not only an individual skill. Read together, they suggest that the question for AI in education is not whether students converse with machines, but who does the explaining. Drawing on my own failed classroom experiment with an AI tutor, and on the innovation that followed—a scalable oral assessment I call the conversational exam, which restores the learner’s voice—I will argue for using AI as an amplifier of human conversation, and for investing in educators as the designers of those conversations.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Building on prior studies that have documented the dehumanization of the users of artificial intelligence (AI) technology, that is, the tendency for observers to attribute less humanness to individuals who use AI than to those who do not, the present research examines whether and how different AI use purposes (i.e., accuracy- vs. efficiency-driven use) influence this effect. We conducted four preregistered studies (total N = 1,270) spanning diverse professional domains. We observed that accuracy-driven AI use negatively predicted the dehumanization of AI users, whereas efficiency-driven AI use positively predicted such dehumanization (Study 1). Furthermore, accuracy-driven AI users elicited less dehumanization than their efficiency-driven counterparts did, a pattern that proved robust across both intuitive assessments of dehumanization (Study 2) and deliberative ratings of humanness traits (Studies 3 and 4). However, both accuracy- and efficiency-driven AI users were significantly dehumanized compared with non-AI users (Study 4), demonstrating that while purpose matters, AI user dehumanization persists. These findings extend the literature on the social cost of AI and offer novel insights into how human–AI interaction shapes interpersonal dynamics .
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

Background/Objectives: Healthcare AI systems described as agentic may improve selected tasks, but gains can reflect models, information access, human support or complete intervention packages. We mapped clinical utility, safety and workflow consequences while distinguishing functional agency from evidence isolating its contribution. Methods: We searched PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, Scopus and Web of Science, supplemented by citation searches, through 11 September 2026. Eligible evidence comprised original empirical journal reports of healthcare systems described as agentic or demonstrating potentially agentic functions. Two authors independently screened records, and two independently extracted data, with adjudication. All four authors jointly assigned analytical classifications after a five-report pilot. A structured critical audit and descriptive Clinical Agency Evidence Chain informed synthesis. The review was not registered. Results: The corpus included 123 reports; 90 were classified as core or bounded functionally agentic. Within this subset, technical task performance was the endpoint category in 44/90 reports (48.9%), and clinical decision/process outcomes in 33/90 (36.7%). Three randomised reports in the broader corpus assessed patient health outcomes: one core, one boundary/non-agentic and one indeterminate. All evaluated bundled interventions. Evidence isolating agency and following its consequences within the same comparison was limited. Safety ascertainment, intended-user error correction and whole-pathway workload were incompletely reported. External or temporal validation occurred in 6/90 reports (6.7%), with partial validation in seven others. Predominantly retrospective, simulated or offline evidence limited clinical inference. Conclusions: Intervention-level benefit must be distinguished from the incremental contribution of agency. Technical gains and local or estimated time savings do not establish patient benefit or reduced total human work. Mechanistic comparisons and prospective clinical evaluations address complementary questions. Adoption decisions should consider benefits, harms, implementation conditions and uncertainty.

documents.abstract: Purpose This study investigates the role of artificial intelligence (AI) as a corporate communicator and examines how AI source transparency influences message credibility, employee trust, employee engagement and ultimately brand advocacy. Specifically, the study explores both cognition-based and affect-based dimensions of trust and evaluates the moderating role of AI literacy in shaping employees’ responses to AI-generated communication. Design/methodology/approach A quantitative research design was adopted using an online survey questionnaire. Data were collected from 317 employees across different organizations who had experience with AI-mediated communication in their workplace. Structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS 4.0 was applied to test the proposed relationships and evaluate the conceptual framework. Findings The findings indicate that AI source transparency positively affects message credibility. Message credibility significantly enhances both cognition-based and affect-based trust, which subsequently increase employee engagement. Employee engagement was also found to positively influence brand advocacy. However, AI literacy showed an unexpected negative moderating effect on the relationship between message credibility and cognition-based trust, suggesting that employees with greater AI knowledge become more critical and skeptical of AI-generated content, whereas its moderating effect on the relationship between message credibility and affect-based trust is not statistically significant. Practical implications Organizations should not use AI solely as an automation tool but also as a strategic communication instrument. Transparency regarding AI usage, combined with human oversight and quality assurance mechanisms, can strengthen credibility and trust. Companies should also invest in content governance and monitoring practices to ensure that AI-generated communication remains accurate, relevant, and aligned with organizational values. Originality/value This study contributes to the growing literature on AI-mediated corporate communication by developing and empirically testing an integrated model linking AI transparency, message credibility, trust, engagement and brand advocacy. It also provides novel insights into the complex role of AI literacy in influencing employee perceptions and trust toward AI-generated communication.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping academic learning by enabling students to delegate cognitively demanding tasks, raising questions about the preservation of student agency and independent learning capacities within sustainable higher education. This study examines whether AI literacy is associated with learning autonomy primarily through critical AI evaluation, responsible AI use, and cognitive offloading rather than through a direct relationship alone. Survey data from 2111 university students in Serbia, the United Kingdom, and Germany were analyzed using structural equation modeling, serial mediation, and multi-group comparisons. AI literacy was positively associated with critical AI evaluation, which was positively related to responsible AI use. Responsible AI use was positively associated with learning autonomy and negatively associated with cognitive offloading, while cognitive offloading was negatively related to learning autonomy. Both serial indirect pathways were significant, whereas the direct association between AI literacy and learning autonomy was nonsignificant. No statistically significant differences in the examined relationships were detected across the three national samples. The findings extend research on sustainable AI-supported higher education by distinguishing technological competence from the evaluative and behavioral practices associated with student agency. They highlight cognitive delegation as an important dimension of the relationship between GenAI engagement and self-reported learning autonomy, offering insights into educational practices that seek to integrate technological assistance while supporting independent reasoning.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming higher education by influencing teaching, learning, assessment, research, academic administration, and student support. In India, this transformation has gained particular significance following the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, which emphasises technology-enabled education, multidisciplinary learning, creativity, critical thinking, skill development, and preparation for an evolving knowledge economy. The emerging concept of Education 5.0 further emphasises human-centred, ethical, sustainable, and collaborative relationships between people and intelligent technologies. However, successful AI integration in Indian higher education depends not only on technological availability but also on AI readiness, technology acceptance, digital pedagogical competence, self-regulated learning, institutional support, and ethical awareness. This study examines the relationships among AI readiness, AI acceptance, AI-supported digital pedagogy, self-regulated learning, and learner engagement within the context of Indian higher education. A convergent mixed-methods design was employed. Quantitative data were collected through validated questionnaires from 250 higher-education teachers and students, while qualitative data were obtained through semi-structured interviews with 20 participants. Quantitative data were examined using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, and multiple regression analysis, while qualitative data were analysed through thematic analysis. The findings indicate positive relationships among AI readiness, AI acceptance, digital pedagogy, self-regulated learning, and learner engagement. The qualitative findings highlight the potential of AI for personalised learning, feedback, academic support, and independent learning while also identifying concerns related to academic integrity, data privacy, misinformation, overdependence, unequal access, and institutional preparedness. The study proposes an India-sensitive framework in which AI readiness functions as a foundation for responsible AI acceptance and pedagogical transformation. The paper concludes that advancing Education 5.0 in Indian higher education requires coordinated investment in AI literacy, faculty development, digital infrastructure, ethical governance, inclusive access, curriculum transformation, and human-centred pedagogical innovation.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can improve students’ work, but an AI-assisted answer does not show whether they can reason alone. This quasi-experiment examined whether tax reasoning demonstrated with AI assistance was maintained when 41 Business Administration students reconstructed it independently. In a digital economy taxation case, the experimental group (n = 20) used the TaxDigital Tutor, an AI tutor developed for this study that guides reasoning without supplying answers, whereas the control group (n = 21) could use generative AI and other resources. All students immediately reconstructed their reasoning by hand without assistance, and both phases were scored with the same five-criterion rubric. Overall, scores were 14.3 points lower in the unassisted reconstruction (F(1, 39) = 18.39, p < 0.001). Scores declined by 17.9 points in the control group (p < 0.001) and by 10.6 points in the experimental group (p = 0.060); however, the exploratory between-group comparison was not significant (p = 0.282). Using case data as evidence was the lowest-scoring criterion in both phases. These findings suggest that scores obtained with AI do not necessarily reflect performance without it. The study also proposes the From Assisted to Autonomous (A2A) framework for progressively reducing AI assistance and assessing independent performance.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in digital food-commerce environments, where frontline employees interact with AI-enabled technologies to support transaction accuracy, service delivery, and operational decision-making. However, limited research explains how employees’ everyday work with AI-enabled systems translates into performance through operational and psychological mechanisms. Drawing on Conservation of Resources (COR) theory and Job Demands–Resources (JD-R) theory, this study examines the relationships between AI-enabled food-service technology, error reduction, psychological empowerment, and in-role performance. Survey data were collected from 410 full-time frontline employees, who evaluated the AI-enabled system they used in their own work, working in chain restaurants in Egypt using convenience sampling and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The findings indicate that AI-enabled food-service technology is positively associated with error reduction, psychological empowerment, and employee performance. Error reduction is positively associated with psychological empowerment and performance, while psychological empowerment is positively associated with performance. Furthermore, error reduction mediates the relationships between AI-enabled technology and both psychological empowerment and employee performance. Error reduction and psychological empowerment also sequentially mediate the relationship between AI-enabled technology and employee performance. These findings extend understanding of employee–AI work interaction in digitally mediated food-service environments by demonstrating how technology-supported accuracy and employees’ psychological resources are associated with effective task performance. The study offers theoretical and managerial implications for integrating AI into digital commerce operations while maintaining employee empowerment and effective human involvement in technology-supported service delivery.

Artificial intelligence (AI) offers a unique opportunity for language education. Speaking anxiety is one of the emotional barriers to learning a second language. As a result of advances in AI-mediated communication technology, second language learners can interact with AI systems through computer-generated conversational agents. However, there has been limited research on the effects of conversing with AI systems on students’ emotional responses, language learning behavior, and willingness to communicate (WTC) from a qualitative and learner-oriented perspective. In an effort to qualitatively explore how AI-mediated communication impacts learners’ sense of psychological safety and language learning behavior, this study recruited 80 undergraduate students who were enrolled in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) courses and had reported moderate to high levels of speaking anxiety. Participants completed four consecutive weeks of structured speaking tasks using the AI technology and completed reflective journals and semi-structured interviews. Reflexive thematic analysis was used to code the qualitative data to discern themes among participants’ responses and experiences. The study’s findings revealed that learners felt AI-mediated communication provided them with a psychologically safe, low-stakes space that led to less anxiety, more emotional comfort, and increased willingness to take linguistic risks. Learners also perceived themselves as taking more risks by using more complicated linguistic forms and feeling more comfortable communicating. The researchers from another study conducted by Jiaohui Tang et al. found that grit, self-efficacy for speaking English, enjoyment of speaking, and speaking anxiety were factors that had an effect on students’ WTC with AI. This can provide further insight into how psychological aspects of learners can impact language learning when AI is involved. From a pedagogical perspective, this suggests that technology like AI can act as a supplement to in-person instruction by providing a preparation space that encourages positive emotional and linguistic risk-taking.

As generative artificial intelligence enters social media marketing, content presentation and posting source have become key cues in users' evaluations of product recommendations. Drawing on the technology acceptance model, this study examines AI-generated content (AIGC) in text-and-image product recommendation posts on Xiaohongshu. It investigates the relationships of perceived anthropomorphic style, perceived informational style, and posting source with prosumption intentions, testing the specific and serial mediating roles of perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness. Three scenario-based studies were analyzed using regression and bootstrapping techniques to ensure robust statistical validation. The results indicate that both style perceptions were positively associated with prosumption intentions, and the official-source materials group reported significantly higher overall intentions than the individual-source group. Furthermore, models estimated separately for each style perception and posting source supported the specific indirect paths through perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness, as well as the serial path through ease of use followed by usefulness. For the product terms between each style perception and posting source, only the indirect path through perceived usefulness was supported. These findings explain users' acceptance of AI-generated product recommendation posts in terms of content comprehension and decision-related evaluations, offering practical guidance for content design and the assessment of marketing effectiveness in the digital era.

The rapid emergence of autonomous artificial intelligence agents, predictive supply chain orchestration, and real-time cross-border regulatory analytics is fundamentally transforming how multinational enterprises (MNEs) govern global value chains (GVCs) and enter foreign markets. Yet International Business (IB) higher education remains largely tethered to twentieth-century pedagogical paradigms—relying on static international trade models, retrospective written case studies, and essentialist cultural heuristics that fail to prepare graduates for algorithmically mediated global commerce. Moving beyond surface-level classroom adoption of generative chatbots, this study develops a comprehensive theoretical and operational framework for re-engineering International Business education through the lenses of Global Value Chain Governance Theory, Activity Theory, and Metacognitive Scaffolding. We argue that the defining competency for next-generation IB professionals is Algorithmic Value-Chain Orchestration—the ability to align predictive and generative AI systems with cross-jurisdictional institutional realities, geopolitical risks, and culturally grounded human judgment. To operationalize this capability, the paper introduces a Three-Horizon Curricular Transformation Architecture alongside a Synthetic Global Commerce Laboratory that immerses students in dynamic multi-tier supply chain disruptions, automated customs and rules-of-origin auditing, and cross-cultural digital platform governance. Drawing upon longitudinal pedagogical implementations across undergraduate and postgraduate IB cohorts, we demonstrate significant gains in students' systemic risk reasoning, critical verification of algorithmic outputs, and cross-border strategic adaptability. Finally, the study examines structural challenges—including cognitive atrophy, Western-centric training data biases, and cross-border data compliance—and establishes an institutional governance charter for sustainable business school transformation.

documents.abstract: Algorithmic management (AM)—the use of algorithms and data-driven systems to allocate, monitor, evaluate and discipline work—has expanded from platform labor into conventional organizations and is increasingly linked to employee well-being. This review maps 255 publications from the reference corpus supplied for this study (nominal window 2020–2026) by combining a transparent title-level text-mining workflow, a behavioral-science coding frame and a reference-by-reference narrative synthesis in which every record is discussed. Methods: titles were parsed, tokenized and screened with stop-word removal; term and bigram frequencies, six theme codes and theme co-occurrence were computed, and the records were then synthesized in seventeen thematic sections covering conceptual foundations, platform-worker evidence, double-edged effects, autonomy, technostress, surveillance, fairness, trust, behavioral outcomes, AI adoption, AI-based well-being tools, careers, Industry 5.0 and sectoral contexts. Results: output is strongly recent (175 of 255 records, 69%, fall in 2025–2026), and the literature concentrates on well-being, burnout and stress (152 titles), AI-enabled HRM and analytics (107) and gig/platform work (68), whereas fairness, transparency and ethics are comparatively less studied (22). The synthesis shows that effects are conditional: algorithmic control can exhaust or energize depending on appraisal, autonomy, fairness, support and the specific control dimension, and that dignity-related pathways complement stress pathways. Conclusions: AM research is dominated by outcome-focused studies of stress and well-being, with ethical and design-oriented work lagging behind; future studies should test moderators such as autonomy and explainability with full-text corpora, longitudinal designs and harmonized measurement.

This study presents an intelligent decision support system (IDSS) that integrates the extreme gradient boosting algorithm with the six-mechanism risk governance framework, which covers identification, assessment, warning, prevention, response, and accountability, for large-scale water diversion projects. Using real-time data from Internet of Things sensors, hazard logs, and management records, the system enables dynamic risk classification and interpretable early warning. Implemented in the Oujiang Water Diversion Project, the IDSS improves the timeliness of decision-making, strengthens proactive risk response, and supports the closed-loop tracking of high-risk events through human–AI collaboration. The paper also discusses practical limitations and provides guidance for deploying similar IDSSs in public infrastructure contexts.

As we move from Industry 4.0 to Industry 5.0, fully automated systems start to give way to human-centric ones, in which human traits such as creativity and problem solving are leveraged and augmented through AI assistance. Human-AI collaboration is therefore fundamental. However, industrial processes are becoming increasingly complex. They are now hyper-connected ecosystems, integrating IIoT, AI, robotics or digital twins with new data streams and interdependencies. For a human, extracting and analyzing data from this complex ecosystem so that informed decisions can be taken becomes a non-trivial challenge. In this paper, we propose an agent-based architecture to interact with a Digital Twin, using FlexSim and a middleware layer as an interface. By leveraging the natural language understanding capabilities of LLMs, the system enables users to interact with the Digital Twin through intuitive, complex queries, democratizing access to data-driven insights and empowering human decision-making. A representative case study is used to provide an early validation of the middleware layer.

documents.abstract: This article presents a methodological proposal grounded in Project-Based Learning (PBL), implemented in secondary education, with the aim of strengthening students’ intrinsic motivation, participation, and deep learning. The study was developed from a qualitative approach through participatory action research, which made it possible to analyze and transform the traditional pedagogical practices of seven teachers in a public educational institution located in a municipality in Colombia. The experience was structured in four phases: diagnosis, planning, implementation, and evaluation. The results show an increase in student motivation, greater cooperation among teachers, and a reduction in failure rates. Likewise, the findings indicate that PBL fosters the satisfaction of basic psychological needs—autonomy, competence, and relatedness—which are essential foundations of human motivation and enhance deep learning, knowledge transfer, and school persistence. Consequently, PBL emerges as a relevant pedagogical strategy for promoting holistic and humanizing education, capable of connecting knowledge with students’ real and meaningful contexts.

Relevance. Software systems that process sensitive data are designed on the assumption that every component performs a predefined operation after an authorisation check. An artificial intelligence (AI) agent, in which a large language model (LLM) selects and calls tools autonomously, does not satisfy this assumption: each decision is made by a probabilistic model based on text, part of which comes from unverified sources. In applications that integrate an LLM, the clear separation of data from instructions disappears. In the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025, prompt injection is ranked first and excessive agency is a separate risk.

Team performance has been extensively theorized in military, healthcare, sports, and organizational domains, yet the extent to which these theories transfer to cyber teams has not been systematically established. Through a systematic review of traditional team performance research and a structured comparison to the current cyber-team evidence, this study addresses that gap. We followed PRISMA 2020 guidance and extracted data from 267 primary studies published between 2015 and 2025 across organizational, project, sports, health care, military and technology-mediated team settings comprising 798 relationship records and 644 unique factor-pair associations spanning 60 standardized factors. The resulting factor inventory and relationship network were then compared against a published set of 42 cyber-team factors using a five-category correspondence rubric, which two coders applied independently (κ = 0.78 for cross-corpus mapping; κ = 0.84 for extraction). Findings demonstrate broad convergence at the factor level: communication, coordination, leadership, trust, shared mental models, and cohesion show strong conceptual correspondence across the traditional and cyber-team literatures, although their operational forms vary with technological mediation, temporal pressure, distributed work, and adversarial conditions. Several well-established traditional-team constructs remain underrepresented in cyber-team research. We integrate these results into a four-layer associative pathway model organizing structural inputs, mediating processes, emergent states, and multidimensional outcomes, and use it to identify where cyber-team theory should extend rather than replace traditional team science. Because the cyber comparison base is weighted toward software engineering, findings are most directly applicable to cyber-relevant technical teams but require further testing in security operations, incident response, and human–AI teaming contexts.

The relevance of the study is due to the fact that the emerging information (digital) technologies, which are now an inevitable reality, have an impact on both society as a whole and the individual modern person, and in many cases have already become part of the latter's daily life. This process is manifested, among other things, in the widespread use of digital technologies, neural networks, intelligent systems, and so on. Artificial intelligence (AI) occupies a special place in this list. Today, there is hardly any area of society or human activity that is not affected by this technological advancement. This also applies to the legal sphere, one of the sections of which is the field of human and civil rights and freedoms. Taking into account the above, the goal of the research can be defined as a comprehensive analysis of all aspects related to: 1) the use of artificial intelligence in various spheres of the state and society; 2) the observance of human and civil rights in the context of the diverse and multifaceted use of AI as a factor influencing the observance of human and civil rights and freedoms both at the domestic and international levels. During our research, we concluded that it is necessary to create a clear regulatory framework that will ensure a balance between the use of AI, on the one hand, and the protection of public interests, as well as human and civil rights and freedoms, on the other. An example of such a framework, in particular, could be the legal regulation of artificial intelligence. By means of the said regulation, it is necessary to keep the process of using AI in various fields and spheres under constant control, and this process itself must be approached very carefully (as is the case with any achievement of scientific and technological progress): 1) to avoid the occurrence of negative consequences and side effects, 2) with the aim of clearly appropriate boundaries of the said use, 3) so that AI truly becomes a real assistant to humans, and not a substitute for human intelligence.

Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains a leading cause of global cancer-related mortality, driven by an ongoing etiological shift toward metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). While early detection is vital for curative intervention, traditional surveillance and diagnostic modalities offer limited sensitivity due to operator dependence and inter-observer variability. This narrative review provides a comprehensive synthesis of emerging and investigational artificial intelligence (AI) applications across different stages of HCC management, ranging from research-stage predictive models to AI-assisted clinical tools. AI-driven radiomics workflows convert complex, non-invasive imaging profiles into high-dimensional data, enhancing the preoperative prediction of microvascular invasion (MVI) and refining standardized Liver Imaging Reporting and Data System (LI-RADS) classifications. Complementing radiology, computational pathology leverages deep learning and emerging pathological foundation models to standardize oncological scoring, mitigate inter-observer variability, and automate histological tumor segmentation. Multimodal AI fusion networks further bridge macroscopic imaging phenotypes with microscopic pathomic signatures and molecular profiles. At the population level, machine learning algorithms optimize dynamic surveillance by integrating longitudinal clinical data with liquid biopsy biomarkers, with the aim of detecting molecular change before it becomes visible on imaging. This review additionally examines AI integration within prospective clinical trial frameworks, encompassing endpoint standardization, patient stratification, and treatment response prediction. While technical challenges including scanner variability and retrospective validation gaps persist, explainable AI (XAI) and federated learning represent the next critical frontier for establishing transportable, accountable digital oncology workflows. Most current applications remain at the technical-validation stage and come largely from single-center, retrospective cohorts. Externally validated models are fewer, and evidence that AI improves clinical decisions or patient outcomes is still very limited.

documents.abstract: BACKGROUND When students perceive artificial intelligence (AI) as a threat to their career prospects (an environmental factor), this perception may elicit self-doubt (a cognitive factor), which in turn may lead to avoidance of academic challenges (a behavioral response), ultimately contributing to anxiety or depression (psychological outcomes). However, to date, the literature lacks empirical evidence supporting this viewpoint within university student samples. AIM To explore the associations between multidimensional AI attitudes and mental health outcomes among Chinese university students, and to examine the nonlinear relationships and the mediating role of self-efficacy in these associations. METHODS A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 2736 undergraduate students from China. Linear regression, restricted cubic spline (RCS) analysis, and path analysis were applied to examine the relationships between AI attitudes (anxiety, job insecurity, self-doubt, and procrastination), self-efficacy, and mental health outcomes (anxiety, depression, stress, loneliness, suicidal ideation, and non-suicidal self-injury). RESULTS Students’ AI attitudes showed a differentiated structure, characterized by low anxiety (9.5%), high job insecurity (50.4%), and moderate levels of self-doubt (25.6%) and procrastination (36.8%). All four AI attitude dimensions positively predicted poor mental health, with procrastination emerging as the strongest predictor. The RCS analysis revealed heterogeneous nonlinear relationships: AI-related anxiety showed nonlinearity for most outcomes, self-doubt and procrastination only for severe outcomes, while job insecurity exhibited stable linearity. Path analysis confirmed that self-efficacy played a partial mediating role in the AI attitude-mental health link. CONCLUSION AI attitudes are associated with complex linear and nonlinear impacts on university students’ mental health, with self-efficacy serving as a key mediating mechanism. These correlational findings provide an empirical reference for targeted mental health interventions and AI literacy education in higher education settings.

documents.abstract: This study examined artificial intelligence integration and its relationship with self-rated instructional planning and assessment construction competency among public elementary school teachers in Zone III, Division of Zambales. A descriptive–correlational survey involved 155 teachers from 12 schools in Cabangan, San Felipe, San Narciso, and San Antonio during school year 2025–2026. Schools were purposively selected, and eligible teachers were included through total enumeration. A researcher-made questionnaire underwent expert review and pilot reliability testing. Descriptive statistics, Mann–Whitney tests, one-way analysis of variance, and Pearson correlations were used. Teachers rated themselves highly competent in instructional planning (mean = 3.65) and assessment construction (mean = 3.59). Artificial intelligence was highly integrated in planning (mean = 3.30) and moderately integrated in assessment construction (mean = 3.02). Learning materials received the highest planning integration rating, while feedback received the lowest assessment rating. Planning and assessment competencies were strongly correlated (r = .823, p < .001). Planning-related artificial intelligence use showed small positive associations with planning competency (r = .180–.249). Use for creating assessments and designing rubrics was significantly associated with assessment competency, but use for analyzing results and providing feedback was not. Selected differences occurred across educational attainment, position, and compensation groups. The findings support professional learning focused on differentiation, assessment review, and feedback. They do not establish that artificial intelligence improves teacher competency. A proposed action plan offers a basis for further implementation and evaluation.

Background/Objectives: Nurses’ medical artificial intelligence (AI)-based innovative behavior may contribute to the effective application of medical AI in clinical practice and the improvement of nursing care. This study examined whether medical explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) was indirectly associated with nurses’ medical AI-based innovative behavior through trust in medical AI and whether medical AI information disclosure moderated the association between medical XAI and trust in medical AI. Methods: A two-wave time-lagged survey with a two-month interval was conducted among 389 nurses from three hospitals in Anhui Province, China. Medical XAI and medical AI information disclosure were measured at Wave 1, whereas trust in medical AI and medical AI-based innovative behavior were measured at Wave 2. Mediation, moderation, and moderated mediation analyses were conducted using Hayes’ PROCESS macro (Models 4 and 7) with 5000 bootstrap resamples. Results: Medical XAI was positively associated with trust in medical AI (B = 0.28, SE = 0.04, 95% CI [0.20, 0.36], p < 0.001), which, in turn, was positively associated with medical AI-based innovative behavior (B = 0.24, SE = 0.05, 95% CI [0.14, 0.34], p < 0.001). The indirect association through trust in medical AI was significant (B = 0.07, BootSE = 0.02, 95% bootstrap CI [0.03, 0.10]). Medical AI information disclosure moderated the association between medical XAI and trust in medical AI (B = 0.08, SE = 0.04, 95% CI [0.01, 0.16], p < 0.05). Specifically, this association was not significant at a low level of medical AI information disclosure (B = 0.04, SE = 0.06, 95% CI [−0.07, 0.16], p > 0.05) but was positive at a high level (B = 0.16, SE = 0.06, 95% CI [0.04, 0.27], p < 0.01). The index of moderated mediation was significant (index = 0.02, BootSE = 0.01, 95% bootstrap CI [0.01, 0.05]). Conclusions: These preliminary findings suggest that trust in medical AI may represent a link between medical XAI and nurses’ medical AI-based innovative behavior and that this indirect association may be stronger at higher levels of medical AI information disclosure. Although the findings should be interpreted as associations rather than causal evidence, they may offer initial insights for technology providers, hospital administrators, and medical institutions.

documents.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (AI) performs tasks once regarded as markers of human intelligence, how people judge the capacities of machines has become a question for intelligence research. This study examined perceived machine agency, the attribution of intelligence-related capacities such as thinking, planning, moral judgment, and problem solving to robots. We tested whether it is associated with psychological distress through AI anxiety and whether self-reported AI literacy moderates this pathway. A convenience sample of 1205 Chinese college students, mainly from Jiangsu Province, completed a cross-sectional survey. Controlling for gender, age, and subjective socioeconomic status, perceived machine agency was significantly but weakly associated with psychological distress. This association was indirect through AI anxiety, and the direct association was not significant. AI literacy significantly moderated the first stage of the indirect association, which became stronger as AI literacy increased. These cross-sectional findings describe associations rather than causal effects. They suggest that attributing intelligence-related capacities to machines is linked to students’ emotional well-being and that greater self-reported AI competence does not by itself weaken this link.

documents.abstract: Mobile autonomous robots are increasingly present in everyday environments, where their sounds play a key role in situational awareness and acceptance. Nevertheless, human responses to robot noise remain underexplored. This study examined how robot operating modes and added alerting sounds affect auditory localization and subjective ratings for a professional cleaning robot. Recordings of the robot operating at two velocities during cleaning and non-cleaning were presented. The non-cleaning mode was additionally combined with multi-tone and noise alerting signals, each with and without amplitude modulation. In a VR experiment with within-subjects design, 27 participants performed a localization task and rated annoyance, valence, arousal, and trustworthiness. Localization performance did not differ significantly between sound conditions. Exploratory post hoc analyses indicated that differences between sound conditions varied with participants’ general localization performance, yielding hypotheses for future studies on the role of baseline localization performance. The cleaning sound was rated as most annoying, least pleasant, and least trustworthy, whereas differences between the non-cleaning conditions were rather small. Overall, the alerting signals did not reliably improve localization under the present listening conditions, but some variants may nevertheless warrant further investigation due to their limited negative effects on subjective ratings.

Artificial intelligence for combinatorial optimization depends on high-quality, structured training data, yet transforming ambiguous natural-language descriptions into precise, executable formal models remains a major bottleneck, traditionally requiring extensive manual effort and domain expertise. We develop CPAM-LLM, an automated constraint-programming modeling framework based on large language models that converts unstructured problem specifications into validated and executable formal models. The framework integrates retrieval-augmented generation grounded in formal concept analysis for structural validation, chaos-mapping-based data augmentation to enhance cross-domain generalization, and dynamic constraint adaptation to accommodate evolving problem settings. We demonstrate its effectiveness across five scenarios, including DNA sequence design, reconfigurable energy storage systems, and unmanned vehicle logistics. The results show that the framework can automate the data-to-model pipeline while adapting reliably to changing requirements, providing a practical approach to automated data formalization and indicating the importance of accessible, high-quality structured data for reliable downstream artificial intelligence applications.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and laboratory automation now operate inside the core loop of physics research. They design optical experiments, shape fusion plasmas, decode quantum errors, select particle collisions in real time and propose new crystals. Existing reviews catalogue these applications by subfield, yet none measures how much decision authority each system holds or how rigorously its outputs are checked. This study introduces two ordinal scales, the Physics Research Autonomy Levels (PRAL, L0 to L5) and the Verification Levels (VL, V0 to V5), and applies them to sixteen documented systems published between 2016 and 2025 in quantum, plasma, particle, gravitational, condensed matter, materials and atmospheric physics. Each system is coded across six research stages: hypothesis, design, execution, analysis, interpretation and reporting. Three results follow. First, autonomy has advanced furthest in execution, where five physics systems act without per-decision human approval, while hypothesis selection and interpretation remain largely human. Second, reported gains concentrate on closed tasks with a fixed objective and a checkable answer, with accelerations from 16 to 2 billion times and equation recovery of 100%, whereas the strongest language model solves 5.7% of open research-level physics challenges. Third, autonomy and verification show no significant association across the corpus (Spearman rho = 0.14, p = 0.59). All four systems whose autonomy exceeds their verification by two or more levels act in hypothesis, design or interpretation, while no system confined to execution or analysis shows such a deficit. This difference is defined here as the verification gap. A Verification-Proportional Reporting checklist is proposed that scales evidence requirements with autonomy. The analysis indicates that the binding constraint on AI-driven physics has shifted from computational capability to verification capacity.

documents.abstract: Digital technologies, including analytics, algorithmic monitoring and generative artificial intelligence (AI), shape how organisations manage creative work, yet their implications for workplace sustainability remain insufficiently integrated in the existing literature. This perspective develops a process-based creativity management framework through a purposive synthesis of research on creativity, information systems, AI and workplace sustainability. An affordance perspective identifies actor-dependent possibilities for action, while a paradox perspective interprets tensions between augmentation and constraint that may recur across projects. The framework links four managerial functions (planning, organising, motivating and controlling) to digital affordances, tensions and proposed managerial conditions, with generative AI treated as a cross-cutting technology. It distinguishes gains in managerial information from employees’ autonomy, intrinsic motivation and willingness to share tentative ideas, while recognising constraints arising from the organisation of joint ideation. Six testable propositions specify actors and mechanisms at individual and team levels; the sixth links functions across project cycles. The theoretical contribution is to show how function-specific tensions may compound across project cycles and affect the psychological conditions that sustain creative work. Practically, the framework identifies configuration choices for feedback, monitoring, analytics and AI-assisted ideation, distinguishing short-term output gains from the long-term capacity of employees and teams to sustain creativity and well-being.

Organizations now have access to unprecedented compute, generative AI tools, multi-agent workflows, and data analytics capabilities, yet most AI initiatives fail to produce measurable transformation. This paper draws on sixteen transcribed sessions of the Barton College Data Analytics Consortium (October 2025–June 2026), a group of educators and practitioners in higher education, data science consulting, and industrial engineering, read alongside change-management, behavioral, and AI-productivity literature. We argue that the primary bottleneck to AI-driven transformation is neither financial nor technical but organizational: the human behavior that resists change. We identify eight distinct sources of resistance grouped into three families (threat-based, principled, and experiential), describe a “fluency trap” in which polished AI output suppresses scrutiny, and show that data literacy is a frequently missing prerequisite for AI readiness. Case evidence contrasts the automation of existing tasks with genuine agentic redesign of work. We conclude with a three-step framework for adoption (fix the process first, commit to scaling rather than downsizing, and run low-stakes, high-visibility pilots) and argue that without confronting behavioral inertia, organizations do not innovate; they simply produce, in one author’s words, “a digital version of a crappy process.”

documents.abstract: Generative AI (Gen AI) has exposed and intensified a long-standing gap between academic products, such as papers and presentations, and the learning processes those products are often assumed to represent. The gap between process and product was always there, and had been widening for a while. This article examines how several pre-AI frameworks no longer adequately account for this shift. We first review earlier efforts to expand Bloom’s cognitive focus, including the models of Marzano and Kendall and L. Dee Fink. We then examine post-AI frameworks such as Michelle Kassorla’s Inverted Bloom’s Taxonomy and Tina Austin’s UnBlooms™ framework. Together, these frameworks suggest that GenAI exposes fundamental weaknesses in existing assessment structures and necessitates a rethinking of how evidence of learning is defined in AI-mediated contexts. How should learning taxonomies and assessment frameworks be reconfigured when GenAI weakens the traditional assumption that academic products reliably demonstrate student learning? Through a conceptual/theoretical analysis of pre-AI and post-AI learning frameworks, we examine how Bloom’s Taxonomy, Marzano and Kendall’s New Taxonomy, Fink’s Significant Learning, Inverted Bloom’s, and UnBlooms™ account for process, product, agency, and metacognition in Higher Education.

BACKGROUND: Correct use of a pressurized metered-dose inhaler (pMDI), usually with a valved holding chamber, depends on use-related conditions that caregivers may not observe directly, including inhalation pattern, actuation-inhalation timing, mask seal, and device orientation. Many digital inhaler systems emphasize actuation or adherence. Systems that infer technique-related conditions from proxy signals may add real-time feedback but also create false reassurance if a positive state is displayed when evidence is inadequate. Caregiver expectations for such feedback and its failure states remain poorly characterized before prototype development. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to characterize caregivers' experiences of pediatric inhaler administration and translate responses to a proposed sensor concept into traceable candidate safety, system, and validation requirements. METHODS: We conducted 23 semistructured concept-elicitation sessions through Zoom videoconference with 27 caregivers of children who currently or previously used a pMDI. Interviews consisted of 19 individual and 4 dyadic sessions pairing 2 caregivers from different households. Sessions were conducted remotely between April and July 2026 from the University of Calgary, Alberta, Canada. Recruitment originated in Calgary and was not geographically restricted. A 6-phase guide examined current practices, difficulties, prior digital-tool use, and responses to a screen-shared clip-on concept incorporating airflow-, timing-, seal-, and orientation-related sensing; on-device feedback; an optional child-facing app; and a caregiver dashboard. No working prototype was evaluated. Approximately 86,000 transcript words underwent hybrid directed and conventional qualitative content analysis using an 18-category codebook. Two researchers independently coded the complete 27×18 matrix (486 paired decisions) across 2 rounds. Consensus categories were translated into candidate requirements and assigned an earliest verification or evaluation locus. Counts are descriptive caregiver-voice tallies, not prevalence estimates. RESULTS: Persistent uncertainty about whether administration conditions were adequate was the dominant lived experience (19/27); for 5 caregivers, existing passive cues had not resolved it. A simple, real-time on-device signal was endorsed by 25 caregivers, but willingness to consider the concept was conditional on reliability (9 caregivers named reasons for abandonment, notably a "false green"), low-friction operation during acute symptoms (12/27), minimal added bulk and technique change, and one or more of clinical validation, clinician recommendation, or a trial pathway (composite category; 23/27). Stances on gamification (20/27), dashboard cadence (18/27), aesthetics (24/27), and privacy (18/27) supported an optional, configurable software layer. Intercoder agreement was 94% (Cohen κ=0.88). The analytic synthesis yielded a conceptual architecture separating observable proxy signals, an inference and data-quality gate, and positive, corrective, or uncertain feedback states. CONCLUSIONS: Participating caregivers prioritized immediate and interpretable feedback about use-related conditions. The findings support conservative state assignment, an explicit uncertain state for indeterminate signals, and app-independent acute-use feedback. These are candidate requirements rather than validated device specifications; subsequent work should proceed through bench verification, simulated-use human factors evaluation, and prospective clinical or field validation.

Generative artificial intelligence complicates the relationship between news credibility and demands for regulation. Caution about substantially AI-generated news need not imply rejection of editorially supervised assistance, while support for accountability need not imply support for unrestricted content controls. This study examines these distinctions in 385 adult, AI-aware questionnaire records supplied as empirical data from Bangladesh. It analyses five separate statements concerning caution, labelling, accuracy accountability, oversight-related trust and proportionate regulation, with supporting awareness and verification items. Low five-item block reliabilities preclude treating the questionnaire as a validated latent-variable model. Analyses combine response distributions, paired contrasts, joint endorsement patterns, rank correlations and exploratory adjusted logistic regression. Accuracy accountability received 84.2% endorsement and oversight-related trust 83.1%, compared with 69.4% for caution, 68.8% for appropriate labelling and 66.8% for proportionate rules respecting lawful expression. Caution and oversight-related trust were jointly endorsed by 57.7%. Accountability exceeded rules endorsement by 17.4 percentage points, while similar aggregate labelling and rules percentages concealed differing responses in 170 records. No selected correlation or focal binary-model coefficient met the 5% threshold after Holm adjustment. The oversight coefficient was positive but sensitive to response coding and sample restriction. The findings distinguish epistemic caution, editorial responsibility and conditional regulatory support rather than demonstrating a causal trust-to-regulation pathway. They support evaluating particular disclosures and oversight procedures against both informational outcomes and expressive rights. Mixed respondent status, undocumented recruitment and fieldwork dates, single-item measurement and unresolved source-documentation labels constrain generalisation. The contribution is an item-specific account of news governance preferences that does not equate favourable survey responses with verified competence or a mandate for coercive regulation.

documents.abstract: Many courses now incorporate online methods for assessing student learning. Some instructors assign questions prior to lecture (e.g., prelecture quizzes) to obtain information that helps them tailor their lessons to the current state of student understanding. To assess curriculum efficacy, physics education researchers often use “pretests,” inventories, etc. that provide baseline data that can be compared to results from post-tests. These assessments were initially given on paper but moved online in the early 2000s. At the University of Washington, we found that the impact of this change was minimal; the results of our pretests stayed essentially the same when given on paper or online and were consistent from quarter to quarter and instructor to instructor. However, we have begun to observe systematic changes in pretest performance that are consistent with students using artificial intelligence (AI) tools to answer pretests, even though they are scored only on effort, not correctness. Using two-proportion z -tests, mixed-effects logistic regression, and Welch’s t tests to analyze response length of explanations, this paper documents the nature and extent of these changes across 39 questions in two introductory algebra-based physics courses. This paper presents results that suggest caution to those using online quizzes to probe student understanding—both before and/or after instruction. We have seen increases in correct responses on pretests as great as 36%, but we have also seen significant decreases on questions that AI tools have tended to answer incorrectly. These findings raise important questions about the validity of online assessments and are intended to raise awareness for anyone using online tests to assess student learning. It remains an open question as to whether, and how, AI can be leveraged to improve instruction.

International students’ psychological adjustment is shaped by challenges involving everyday agency, social connection, and separation from familiar support networks. This study examined short-term changes in psychological wellbeing, social self-efficacy, and homesickness following a 12-day generative artificial intelligence (GenAI)-assisted daily activity programme among Pakistani international students in China. Guided by Self-Determination Theory, the programme combined activities intended to support autonomy, competence, and relatedness with GenAI-assisted planning, reflection, and conversational rehearsal. Twenty-eight participants completed self-report assessments immediately before and after the programme in a single-group pre-test–post-test design. Outcomes were assessed using Ryff’s Psychological Well-Being Scale, a social self-efficacy measure, and the homesickness subscale of the Acculturative Stress Scale for International Students. Reported Wilcoxon signed-rank analyses indicated an increase in overall psychological wellbeing from 86.38 to 98.14 (p = .004) and a decrease in homesickness from 10.90 to 7.52 (p = .002). Social self-efficacy increased from 96.38 to 107.34, although this change was not statistically significant (p = .092). These findings provide preliminary evidence of favourable changes in selected psychosocial outcomes during participation in a structured GenAI-assisted activity programme. However, the absence of a comparison group, the small purposively recruited sample, and the lack of follow-up prevent attribution of these changes to GenAI or conclusions about their durability. The study offers an initial application of need-supportive programme design in a South–South educational mobility context and provides a basis for subsequent controlled evaluation.

documents.abstract: We examined cognitive and attitudinal correlates of trust in AI-generated content in a 2025 cross-sectional survey in Türkiye. The respondent cohort comprised 232 records; 207 self-identified generative AI users completed the focal measures. A hierarchical regression distinguished perceived Generative AI Literacy, behavioral use frequency, positive and negative AI attitudes, an exploratory post-truth index, and risk/regulatory concern. Literacy and frequency explained 0.2% of trust variance; attitudes added 12.2%, and the joint post-truth/concern block added 13.6%. The final model explained 26.0% (adjusted R² = 0.238). Positive attitude (β = 0.310), negative attitude (β = −0.215), and the post-truth index (β = 0.425) had significant conditional associations. Negative attitude had an essentially null zero-order association ( r = .021). The post-truth index uniquely accounted for 13.4% points beyond the other measured predictors. Exploratory structure analyses supported a dominant common dimension but also revealed residual item clustering; content-domain sensitivity analyses localized the association mainly to devaluation of factual truth. Education-group differences did not survive adjustment across six outcome tests. These self-report associations do not establish causality, objective misinformation susceptibility, or a validated unitary post-truth disposition.

documents.abstract: Learning from human demonstrations has emerged as a promising paradigm in robotics. Especially in the context of disassembly tasks in circular factories, this would allow factory workers to teach robotics new skills without the need for robotics engineers or programmers, thus enabling flexible and scalable automation in modern manufacturing systems. However, collecting demonstrations only as a pre-deployment step is not flexible enough for rapidly changing production contexts. In circular manufacturing, end-of-life conditions are revealed during processing, and even in high-mix conventional manufacturing, variants and edge cases evolve faster than static offline datasets. We therefore argue for an integrated train-while-operate approach in which demonstrations are collected during productive operation, and policies are continuously updated. A key challenge of this approach is fluctuating demonstration quality caused by varying operator cognitive workload under real factory demands. This paper addresses this problem with a cognitive-workload-guided dataset-filtering framework for industrial learning from demonstration. We estimate demonstrator cognitive and physical workload during task execution and filter demonstrations collected under elevated workload. The framework is implemented and evaluated in a robot teleoperation scenario where cognitive workload is systematically varied to emulate realistic workload fluctuations and estimated using two sensing systems for comparison. Experimental results show that filtering the dataset with the proposed heuristics improves the performance of the learned motion models.

Generative AI can support students’ learning and problem-solving, yet little is known about whether and how human–AI collaboration changes across social contexts. This study introduces competition as an important social context and examines how it shapes students’ use of AI-generated content in creative problem-solving. A total of 92 undergraduates were randomly assigned to competition or no-competition conditions and completed three creative problem-solving tasks with GenAI support, yielding 276 student-task observations. Semantic similarity analysis, behavioral coding, regression analysis, and permutation tests were used to examine changes in AI-content use and their individual- and collective-level changes. Results showed that competition reduced students’ semantic overlap with AI-generated content and increased almost full rejection of AI suggestions, without a corresponding statistically detectable increase in self-directed improvement. Competition was associated with greater idea fluency and flexibility, but lower fluency-normalized flexibility, and neither individual semantic distinctiveness nor collective semantic diversity consistently increased. Together, these findings distinguish behavioral distancing from constructive human agency in AI-supported problem-solving: using less AI-generated content does not necessarily mean engaging with AI more independently or achieving greater relative diversity. The study therefore highlights human–AI collaboration as a socially situated process and shifts attention from the amount of AI use to the performance of students’ engagement with AI-generated content. Supporting effective AI-assisted learning may require fostering students’ capacity to critically evaluate, transform, and extend AI-generated ideas rather than simply encouraging greater or lesser reliance on GenAI.

This essay takes its point of departure from a short story by the American novelist Laura van den Berg. It argues that van den Berg’s “Samatha” can be read as a “post-speculative realist” allegory for our relationship with emerging AI technologies. In particular, it is concerned with analyzing how the widespread adoption of large language model chatbots is transforming our relationships with ourselves and others. It attempts to describe this experience in terms of a structure that I call “connection without presence.” Connection without presence is an attempt to name the strange, posthuman form of desire that is at work in our relationship with many communications technologies. In terms of the Foucaultian philosophy, it suggests that the chatbot is a confessional wherein the human being whispers their desire to disappear-and learns to enjoy its submission.

AI-generated bug reports have drawn criticism for unreliable claims and faulty reproducers that burden maintainers. However, as LLM capabilities improve, some maintainers have begun to express more positive views on AI use in bug reporting and maintenance. Understanding this evolution requires examining whether AI-involved reports are becoming more reliable, which uses of AI are associated with valid findings, and how maintainers investigate these reports and act on them. To this end, we conduct the first large-scale study of 120,918 bug reports from 101 open-source projects between January 2024 and September 2026, tracing AI involvement from discovery and reporting through validation and resolution. Our findings show that AI-involved reports become more complete over time, with a growing share of reports confirmed as valid. In bug reporting, AI for reproduction and diagnosis are associated with higher validity, whereas report writing is not. Extends into maintenance, maintainers increasingly use AI to investigate code and recommend fixes. However, they devote more effort to AI-assisted reports of human-discovered bugs than to reports of AI-discovered bugs. These findings highlight both AI's growing participation in bug investigation and the continuing need for verification and follow-up. Drawing on these findings, we provide practical guidance for turning AI-generated findings into verifiable reports: emphasizing reproducibility, verification, and accountability. We followed this guidance when submitting 53 reports on AI-discovered bugs, of which 69.81% were accepted by maintainers as of writing.

Recent advances in generative AI have renewed interest in whether large language models can simulate aspects of public deliberation. Current deliberation simulations remain methodologically fragile: fluent conversational outputs are often treated as evidence of deliberative quality despite limited reproducibility, weak safeguards for viewpoint diversity, and limited systematic evaluation. This article argues that AI-deliberation simulations can function as credible analytical instruments only if they incorporate infrastructures for reproducibility, plurality preservation, and deliberative quality assessment. The article develops a stage-structured method for deliberative simulation combining persona validation, plurality auditing, and discourse-quality assessment within a reproducible pipeline. The framework is presented as a methodological proof-of-concept and evaluated through a simulation study on the June 2023 Swiss federal referendum on the Climate and Innovation Act together with a batch replication study comparing direct and structured deliberation architectures. The findings show that, as an integrated theory-driven architecture, the structured pipeline generates more stable deliberative dynamics than unconstrained interaction, including clearer plurality preservation and more coherent opinion updating. At the same time, the simulations remain below human minipublics in terms of contextual grounding and justificatory depth. The article positions AI-deliberation simulations as methodological infrastructures for cumulative and empirically testable research on AI-supported deliberation in digital governance.

documents.abstract: Digital learning environments require pedagogical approaches that address students’ cognitive demands and variability. This scoping review maps how Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) and Universal Design for Learning (UDL) inform the design of digital learning environments across educational contexts, examining design principles, implementation characteristics, research methods, and reported outcomes. Searches were conducted in Scopus, Web of Science, and ERIC. Eligibility criteria focused on empirical journal articles published in English that described, analysed, or evaluated digital environments designed using principles of CLT and/or UDL. Data were organised into a matrix covering study characteristics, theoretical frameworks, design elements, assessment instruments, and findings. The review included 34 studies: 17 were classified as CLT-oriented, 16 as UDL-oriented, and one explicitly combined both frameworks. The environments analysed included learning management systems, MOOCs, multimedia resources, mobile applications, immersive environments, and educational games. CLT-oriented designs emphasised segmentation, cueing, worked examples, and cognitive load management; in contrast, UDL-oriented designs highlighted accessible resources, flexible participation, and multiple means of engagement, representation, and action and expression. Reported outcomes included academic performance, cognitive load, engagement, motivation, accessibility, and usability. Heterogeneity in research designs and assessment measures limits conclusions regarding comparative effectiveness. The mapping identifies limited explicit integration of CLT and UDL and highlights the need for further research into their operational alignment in digital instructional design.

Artificial intelligence (AI) has entered pupils’ daily lives before it has been incorporated into school curricula, yet schools tend to view it either as a risk to be contained or as a productivity tool to be mastered, neglecting pupils’ ability to understand, question and transform the algorithmic systems that shape their experience. This theoretical contribution proposes a conceptual foundation for an engaging AI education, in which algorithmic citizenship is practised through authentic tasks rather than taught as content. The study conducts a critical, integrative literature review that brings together research on school engagement, self-determination theory, authentic learning, AI literacy, and critical data studies, and reinterprets the criteria for authentic learning in light of the distinctive characteristics of algorithmic objects: opacity, mutability, reflexivity, and distributed effects. The analysis identifies three shifts in the classical criteria (from relevance to the real world to relevance to the lived world; from a multiplicity of perspectives to political plurality; and from integrated assessment to intervention) and a framework of design principles structured across three levels, relating to motivational needs, scaffolding and persistence, illustrated by three task scenarios. The paper argues that strong engagement arises when students recognise that the task concerns them and that their own actions can influence it, and it outlines its limitations, ethical issues and hypotheses for empirical research.

Writing a Social Story requires information about the learner and the situation, together with attention to language and accuracy. Generative artificial intelligence may assist with drafting, but its output requires review before educational use. This paper describes a Social Stories™ generation tool developed within the Socrate platform at the University of Salerno as part of a project supporting Individualized Education Plan design. The tool combines a module for collecting educational information with a technical module for configuring generation and review. Users specify the learner’s communication profile, the context, the story’s purpose and available support. A Python backend coordinates language model generation, automated checks and revision, with separate drafting and reviewing roles. The procedures are designed to identify structural problems, unsupported assumptions and coercive or judgmental wording. Teachers retain responsibility for checking the narrative and deciding whether it is appropriate for the learner. Feedback and revision records provide material for professional discussion and training. The paper outlines the tool’s architecture and the evaluation needed to assess narrative quality and educational use. Future work will compare local and general-purpose models through expert assessment and examine whether stories support learners’ understanding in the situations for which they are written.

The trustworthiness of technology constitutes a critical determinant of user adoption, particularly regarding artificial intelligence (AI) in daily life. Currently, prominent AI products rely on large language models (LLMs), and such LLMs assist users in personal and professional contexts. To systematically investigate the perceived trustworthiness of LLMs, we provide a psychometrically sound measurement instrument for assessing perceived trustworthiness of LLMs. Given the importance of the Chinese market for current AI developments, the present study examined the psychometric properties of a Chinese version of the Perceived Trustworthiness of Large Language Models Scale (PT-LLM-8) [1] and its association with Big Five personality traits, self-efficacy, and self-esteem. Based on the responses of 478 Chinese adults, the Chinese PT-LLM-8 showed good psychometric properties, including strong internal consistency and a clear unidimensional factor structure. Evidence of construct validity was provided by theoretically expected associations between PT-LLM-8 score and self-efficacy, self-esteem, Agreeableness, and Conscientiousness. These findings provide psychometric support for the Chinese version of the PT-LLM-8 as a measure of perceived trustworthiness of LLMs, consistent with the cumulative cross-linguistic evidence for the instrument across its English [1], German [2] and Chinese versions.

Thai computer teacher trainees must assemble and repair computers during their practicum, yet many get little hands-on practice because laboratory machines are scarce, outdated, and easily damaged. This design-and-development study built a virtual reality learning environment (VRLE) for computer assembly on a Meta Quest 3 headset, with controller-free hand tracking, three simulation rooms mapped to a national occupational competency unit, and learning media produced with generative AI. Development followed the ADDIE model, and a feasibility tryout used a one-group pretest–posttest design. Three content experts and three technical experts rated content (M = 4.74) and technical quality (M = 4.45) as very good, with interaction and usability the weakest domain (M = 4.11). Among 35 pre-service teachers with matched tests, achievement rose from 8.20 to 9.09 out of 10 (Wilcoxon z = 2.95, p = .002, r = .50; t(34) = 2.92, dz = 0.49). After a sequence of website lessons, VR practice, real-hardware practice, and debriefing, mean competency on real hardware was 4.85 (n = 36) and mean satisfaction was 4.79 (n = 28), both with ceiling effects. Without a control group, the results show that the VRLE is feasible and well received, not that it caused the gains.

Introduction This study examined changes in students' self-reported creativity-related behaviors following an educational intervention combining artificial intelligence (AI) tools and the DRAE instructional model (Diagnosis, Recreation, Application, and Estimation). Methods A one-group preexperimental pretest-posttest questionnaire design was complemented by semi-structured interviews and direct-observation records. The quantitative analysis included 551 valid paired EvaCreIA records, exceeding the minimum sample target of 543. The questionnaire assessed Generate Diverse Ideas (GID), Generate Creative Ideas (GIC), and Evaluate and Improve Ideas (EMI). Complementary interview indicators were calculated from 703 eligible pretest and 730 eligible posttest records, while direct observation included 568 completed checklist records. Results Posttest means exceeded pretest means by 0.222, 0.270, and 0.241 points for GID, GIC, and EMI, respectively, on a five-point scale. Wilcoxon signed-rank comparisons remained statistically significant after Holm adjustment ( p < .001). Rank-biserial correlations were 0.340 for GID, 0.387 for GIC, 0.340 for EMI, and 0.374 for the supplementary overall score. The complementary interview indicators showed higher favorable-response percentages at posttest. Discussion The results indicate changes in self-reported creativity-related behaviors following the combined educational intervention. However, retrospective record linkage, limitations in cross-instrument correspondence, self-report measurement, and the absence of a comparison group restrict causal interpretation. The findings do not establish an independent causal effect of AI or validate the DRAE model.

Role allocation strategies in human-robot collaboration typically assign tasks to both the human and the robot, limiting the user's ability to take initiative. Furthermore, allocation decisions may conflict with the user's intentions, and the rationale behind such allocations may remain unclear, potentially reducing both acceptance and collaboration fluency. The novelty of the proposed framework is that the human is left free to contribute to the task, while the robot is dynamically allocated activities through a cost-driven Behavior Tree architecture according to user-expressed preferences and behavior. Explicit preferences are extracted from natural language instructions using a large language model, whereas human activity is monitored online through a Shannon entropy-based analysis of hand-object interactions. Furthermore, the framework can recognize anomalies in human execution and autonomously trigger corrective robot actions. The approach was validated through a pilot study and a multi-subject experiment involving 14 participants. Results demonstrate the potential of such an allocation strategy for enabling intuitive and engaging collaboration without increasing the perceived workload.
